title: American Airlines 327
summary: During an instrument approach to Tulsa in poor weather with a measured ceiling of only 200 feet and visibility of 1.75 miles, the Convair descended through dense clouds and fog below the safe altitude. The aircraft struck a hillside 3.6 miles north of the runway. The investigation found that the captain's lack of alertness allowed the first officer to continue descent to an altitude too low for terrain clearance.
probable_cause: The captain's lack of alertness in allowing the first officer to continue an instrument descent to an altitude too low to permit terrain clearance.

title: Pacoima aircraft accident

location.name: Pacoima Junior High School, San Fernando Valley, Los Angeles

summary: On January 31, 1957, a Douglas DC-7B on its first functional test flight from Santa Monica collided at 25,000 feet in clear skies with a United States Air Force Northrop F-89J Scorpion fighter jet over the San Fernando Valley. The high-speed, near-head-on collision occurred northeast of the Hansen Dam spillway. The DC-7B, with a portion of its left wing shorn off, remained airborne for about 20 seconds in an uncontrollable spiraling dive before breaking apart. The wreckage struck the Pacoima Congregational Church and the adjacent Pacoima Junior High School playground, killing all four Douglas crew members, two students, and the F-89 pilot.
probable_cause: A Douglas DC-7B and a United States Air Force Northrop F-89J Scorpion converged at 25,000 feet in clear skies over the San Fernando Valley during independent test flights. Investigators determined the two aircraft most likely converged over an area northeast of the Hansen Dam spillway, resulting in a high-speed, near-head-on collision.

title: Northeast Airlines 823
summary: Northeast Airlines Flight 823, a Douglas DC-6, crashed shortly after takeoff from LaGuardia in poor visibility. The captain entered cloud cover and lost spatial awareness on instruments, executing an incorrect left turn instead of the assigned northeast heading. The aircraft descended below terrain clearance and crashed into trees on Rikers Island, killing 20 passengers.
probable_cause: The failure of the captain to properly observe and interpret his flight instruments, and to maintain control of his aircraft.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was flying on instruments without outside visibility as it headed over Flushing Bay.
The captain lost spatial awareness when he entered the clouds seconds after takeoff, therefore didn't detect or correct the airplane's deviation from its desired course.
The airplane began a gradual turn to the left, and when it had reached a heading of 285° (nearly due west), it overflew Rikers Island.
Its altitude was insufficient to clear the trees on the island, and the aircraft crashed.

events.text: Delays due to snowfall pushed departure back; the airplane was cleared to take off via runway 04 at 6:01 PM.
Upon establishing a positive rate of climb, the landing gear and wing flaps were retracted.
Aircraft entered cloud cover flying on instruments without outside visibility.
The aircraft came to rest within 1,500 ft of the point of first impact after crashing into trees on Rikers Island.

title: Sutton Wick air crash
summary: A Blackburn Beverley of No. 53 Squadron RAF departed RAF Abingdon bound for Cyprus carrying cargo and relief personnel. During climb, No. 1 engine developed a fuel leak and was shut down. No. 2 fuel tank showed large losses. On final approach, No. 2 engine failed to respond to throttle inputs. The aircraft became uncontrollable, struck high-tension cables and elm trees that tore the port wing from the fuselage. Of 22 occupants, all but 4 were killed; 2 people on the ground were also killed.
probable_cause: A non-return valve in the fuel system had been installed the wrong way round, causing two engines to be starved of fuel. The technician found responsible for incorrectly fitting the valve was charged under the Air Force Act.

events.text: As the aircraft climbed, No. 1 engine on the port wing developed a fuel leak.

Crew de-activated the fuel cocks and boosters for the No. 2 tank, but left them on for the No. 1 tank.
No. 2 engine failed to respond to throttle inputs and the aircraft began to lose speed and height.
The aircraft struck a number of high tension cables and a group of elm trees that tore the port wing from the fuselage.
The aircraft crashed upside down, 18 minutes after take-off.

title: British European Airways 411
summary: A Vickers Viscount on approach to Manchester Airport experienced metal fatigue in the bottom bolt securing the starboard wing number 2 flap unit, causing that flap to detach in flight. The aileron locked, and the aircraft entered a steep right descending turn with a steep bank angle that the crew could not recover from. The right wing struck the ground one mile short of the runway, and the rest of the plane broke up and burst into flames. All 20 occupants died, and two additional people in a house at the impact point were killed.
probable_cause: Metal fatigue in the bottom bolt securing the starboard wing number 2 flap unit caused the flap to detach, which locked the aileron. The loss of aileron control resulted in an uncontrollable steep right turn that could not be recovered from, leading to ground impact.

title: 1957 Cebu Douglas C-47 crash
summary: A newly reconditioned Philippine Air Force C-47 carrying President Ramon Magsaysay and 25 others crashed on the slopes of Mount Manunggal in Cebu at 1:40 AM on March 17, 1957. The aircraft failed to gain sufficient altitude as it approached mountain ranges in Balamban. The sole survivor was journalist Nestor Mata. An investigation concluded that metal fatigue in the right engine carburetor drive shaft caused power failure shortly after takeoff.
probable_cause: The spindle drive shaft of the right engine carburetor snapped due to metal fatigue, causing a power failure on the aircraft. The crew failed to maintain sufficient altitude during climb over the mountainous terrain, resulting in controlled flight into terrain.

title: LOT Polish Airlines 232
summary: LOT Polish Airlines Flight 232, an Ilyushin Il-14P, crashed near Vnukovo Airport while descending in poor weather after being instructed to descend to 300 meters. The investigation determined the pilot failed to comply with the prescribed instrument approach procedure, descending to an extremely low altitude. The aircraft struck the ground at high speed in very low ceiling conditions with heavy turbulence and rain, killing 9 people including the pilot, co-pilot, and two crew members.
probable_cause: The aircraft hit the ground while flying at an excessively low altitude following the crew's application of an approach procedure other than that prescribed by Vnukovo Aerodrome. title: Varig 850
summary: A Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation operated by Varig departed Ciudad Trujillo in the Dominican Republic with one engine already shut down (engine 2) due to a failure shortly after takeoff from Belém. At 3,000 meters altitude, 50 minutes after departure, engine 4 began to overspeed and the pilot was unable to feather the propeller. The detached propeller from engine 4 struck and damaged engine 3, leaving only engine 1 operational. The crew ditched the aircraft in the Atlantic Ocean near Cabarete. The tail structure separated on impact, killing one flight attendant in the rear section, though the remaining crew was rescued by people on the beach.

title: 1957 Kiev mid-air collision
summary: Two Ilyushin Il-14 aircraft collided over Kyiv on August 17, 1957, killing 15 people. Aeroflot Flight 126 was on approach to Kiev-Zhulyany Airport when it collided with a training flight at about 250-300 meters. The propeller of the Il-14M struck the right wing of the other aircraft. Both aircraft dived into the ground and crashed into several houses 4.5 kilometers from the airport.
probable_cause: The cause was primarily ATC error, specifically the guidance and assistance of the air traffic controller at Kiev-Zhulyany Airport. Aeroflot Flight 126 was not told about the presence of another Il-14 performing training manoeuvres in the area.

title: 1957 Nutts Corner BEA Viscount crash
summary: A BEA Vickers Viscount departing London Heathrow for Belfast Nutts Corner Airport commenced its approach to runway 28 in low cloud and rain conditions. As the aircraft neared the runway, it veered right of the runway centerline. The crew carried out a go-around but the aircraft crashed about 1000 feet to the left of the far end of the runway. All seven people on board were killed. A public inquiry found no official cause but noted that the airport's approach lighting system may have been switched off at the time and a bent screwdriver was found in the wreckage, though its exact position could not be verified.

title: Pan Am 7
summary: Pan Am Flight 7, a Boeing 377 Stratocruiser with 44 aboard, disappeared en route from San Francisco to Honolulu on November 8, 1957. The aircraft made a routine position report at 5:04 p.m. while 1028 nautical miles east of Hawaii but was never heard from again approximately nine hours later when fuel would have been exhausted. No emergency signals were received. The CAB concluded it did not have enough evidence to determine the cause of the accident.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board could not determine the cause of the accident. The aircraft disappeared without any emergency signal after approximately nine hours of flight when fuel reserves would have been exhausted.

factors.evidence: Aircraft had enough fuel for approximately thirteen hours of flight; crash occurred about nine hours after departure when aircraft would have exhausted fuel reserves.
Sabotage and in-flight fire were among theories explored but no definitive evidence found to support these causes.
Poor maintenance was speculated as possible cause, though CAB found aircraft, engines, and propellers had been maintained as prescribed.
Aircraft disappeared with bodies and wreckage eventually recovered, indicating structural failure or loss of control leading to impact with water.

events.text: Flight 7 departed San Francisco International Airport at 11:30 a.m. carrying 36 passengers and 8 crew members, maximum takeoff weight 147000 lb.
Captain made routine position report at 5:04 p.m. while aircraft was 1028 nautical miles east of Hawaii, cruising at 10000 ft altitude with headwinds of approximately 14 mph.
Expected position report around 6:00 p.m. was never received; aircraft disappeared from radar contact without any emergency signal.
After no communication for more than 90 minutes, Pan Am notified Coast Guard; extensive search found 19 bodies and aircraft pieces about 900 nautical miles northeast of Honolulu.

Investigation found the initial number 4 engine failure cause unknown; number 3 failure resulted from either electrical failure in fuel cutoff actuator circuit or accidental cutoff switch operation. Post-impact fire killed 45 of 58 on board.

title: Aerolíneas Argentinas 670
summary: Aerolíneas Argentinas Flight 670, a Douglas DC-4, took off from Buenos Aires on 8 December 1957 bound for San Carlos de Bariloche with 61 occupants. The captain chose to fly at 328 to 492 feet instead of the cleared altitude of 3,937 to 7,874 feet in an attempt to avoid an intense cold front. The aircraft then climbed sharply to 8,202 feet and entered the worsening storm at its most active part. At this height, the left wing failed followed quickly by the tail section, and the aircraft dove uncontrollably into the ground. Investigation determined the aircraft disintegrated from severe turbulence stress after the pilot's reckless decision to fly into the storm.
